DR. MARTIN ZSCHORNAK · DAY

—

Speaking · Halle (Saale), Germany

Dr. Martin
Zschornak

What sound does to people.

Sound can now destroy a liver tumour. No cut. No heat.

A radiation oncologist who has played to crowds on six continents explains how. He talks about what happens in a body when it listens, and he plays the violin on stage while he does it.

Spoken at

  • Singularity Summit South Africa
  • Music Frontiers, Berlin
  • Future of Festivals, Berlin
  • Amsterdam Dance Event
  • Zurich Music Week
  • Universitätsklinikum Halle
01

Evidence from the clinic.

He treats patients, teaches, and is designing two clinical trials on whether sound can lower the fear of lying still in a radiotherapy machine. He is clear about what is known, and where it ends.

Most people who talk about sound have stood in one of two rooms. He has spent fifteen years in both. In the clinic he is a specialist in radiation oncology at the university hospital in Halle.

On stage, as Seth Schwarz, he has played electric violin live over his own sets in 189 cities and 46 countries.

So the talk comes from both rooms: the evidence from one, the instinct from the other, and a violin in his hands when the words run out.

Radiation oncologySpecialist physician, Universitätsklinikum Halle. He teaches there.
DoctorateOn glioblastoma brain tumours.
Clinical trialsHe is designing two clinical trials on sound and anxiety during radiotherapy.
CusanuswerkMerit scholar throughout his medical studies. Research poster prize at OncoRay.
Trained in four countriesRadiation oncology at AKH Vienna with Prof. Pötter and at Acıbadem, Istanbul. Surgery and obstetrics at Hospital Alemán Nicaragüense, 2012/13.
Recording artistAs Seth Schwarz: All Day I Dream, Katermukke, 3000 Grad. The night side of this page.

His own keynote screen. Often credited to Nikola Tesla; no one has found where he said it.

02

Live music inside the talk.

Where another speaker shows a slide, he plays. The room hears the point instead of reading it. In English or German.

Sound is already a medical instrument.

Focused ultrasound, called histotripsy, destroys liver tumours without a cut. Authorised in the US since 2023. It works mechanically, not by heat.

45 min · keynote

What sound does to fear

The clinical one. What is known about sound, attention and anxiety, what is still only promising, and what he plans to test with patients who have to lie still inside a machine. Careful about the evidence and clear about where it ends.

30 to 45 min

Improvisation as a discipline

What twenty years of playing without a plan teaches about judgement under pressure. A delayed flight that became a back-to-back set, a sunrise that could not be rehearsed.

30 min

The instrument and the machine

A classically trained violinist who builds tracks from seventy hand-played parts, on what is gained and lost when a craft meets a machine.

Talk + 60 to 90 min

Talk and closing set

He speaks in the programme and closes the evening on violin and decks. One traveller, two slots. Done at the Singularity Summit.

The problem

Most talks are gone by the coffee break.

  1. They sound alike.He doesn't. A cancer doctor with a violin.
  2. Slides don't move a room.He plays the point instead.
  3. The evening needs a second booking.He is the second booking.

Martin speaks. Seth plays. One booking.

Frequency lab

Same mind, different frequencies.

From the questions of the clinic to the festival drop. Pick a frequency or drag the slider, watch the wave, and listen if you like.

Pitch

Schumann resonance active · 7.83 HzThe Earth’s electromagnetic resonance. Lightning keeps the space between the ground and the ionosphere ringing at about 7.83 Hz, with overtones near 14.3, 20.8, 27.3 and 33.8 Hz. Here those five rates shape a low drone.

A demonstration of frequencies, not a treatment. Theta and gamma play two soft tones a few hertz apart, and you hear their difference as a pulse; 124 BPM plays a quiet kick. The Schumann switch is physics, not medicine. The pitch fader bends every tone, from two octaves down to two octaves up; the − and + buttons move it by a tenth of a semitone. Sound only starts when you press play or flip the switch.

  1. 1Write to him.

Questions

Before you ask.

What does a talk cost?

It depends on the format, the length and the travel. A talk with a closing set is booked together, and costs less than a speaker and a DJ booked separately.

What does he need on stage?

Very little: a headset microphone, a screen, and one more line into the sound system for the violin. He brings the violin. The exact list comes with the confirmation.

Is the science solid?

He separates what is proven from what is only promising, and says so on stage. No healing claims, and the trials are described, never oversold.

What will our audience take home?

One clear idea about sound and the body that they can retell, and a live moment with the violin they will remember.

Publications and press

On the record.

His published research is laboratory work on brain tumour cells. It is not about music. The press pieces are about a doctor who also plays.

DJ · Electric violin · Live

SETH
SCHWARZ

A DJ on six continents. With a violin.

He plays electric violin live over his own DJ set. No band, no backing track. The violin answers the music as it happens, so no two nights sound the same.

189Cities
46Countries
6Continents
20Burns
26M+Plays

Twenty burns: nine Burning Man, ten AfrikaBurn, one Midburn. 26 million plays and views, all counted on 16 November 2026: Spotify’s ten most played tracks, collaborations and remixes included (19.2M); all 130 tracks and sets on his own SoundCloud (5.7M); seventeen sets that live on other people’s SoundCloud accounts, among them the PlayAlchemist opening at Burning Man 2017 with Be Svendsen and Unders (1.1M); twenty-nine videos on YouTube (449K); ten shows on Mixcloud (1.9K). The real figure is higher: Spotify lists only its top ten publicly, and Apple Music, Deezer, Tidal and Beatport publish no play counts at all.

In his words

What 189 cities taught me about a night.

  1. Good music is not rare any more.Every city has DJs who play well. That alone no longer fills a room twice.
  2. Nobody goes home talking about a transition.They talk about the one moment when the whole room looked up.
  3. That moment has to be played, not planned.It is why I bring the violin, and why I never play the same set twice.

Questions

Before you ask.

What does it cost?

It depends on the date, the place, the slot and the travel. Put your budget in the form and the agency answers with one offer. Travel and hotel come on top. Private hosts can ask for one all-in price.

What do we need to set up?

A normal DJ booth: three CDJ-3000s, a DJM-900NXS2 or better, two monitors, a table and power. He brings the violin and his pedalboard. The full rider comes with the offer.

Can we count on him?

Twelve years of shows on Resident Advisor alone. When his flight landed late at Pleinvrees, the night still happened: he and Acid Pauli played it together.

Is it worth it for our event?

People stay. Listeners write that they walked past and stayed for three hours. And the violin is the part they film, so your night travels further than the room.

He plays a few weekends a year. Ask for yours.

He is also a doctor, so he plays selected weekends, not every one. 2027 dates are being planned now.

        The story

        A violinist who became a DJ, and a radiation oncologist.

        Seth Schwarz plays the violin into the heart of electronic music. Classically trained from the age of seven, he played for years in the symphony orchestra in Hoyerswerda, where he was born, and learned to improvise in a jazz band. A night on the dance floor at Fusion Festival in 2009 changed his direction; the following summer he was on its stage.

        He is a DJ first, and a violinist on top. Behind the decks he builds deep, melodic sets of ambient electronica, organic and melodic house and techno; over them he plays, loops and layers his electric violin through effects in real time, so every set is shaped by the room and the moment. His violin today is an NS Design CR-5.

        It started in May 2012 with his debut vinyl, the Magnolia EP. Presenting it live at Charles Bronson in Halle, he found the record thin on its own, so he ran his first electric violin, bought in Nicaragua during a hospital internship, through effect pedals and played over it. Since then he has written more than 150 productions, collaborated with Einmusik, Be Svendsen, Mollono.Bass, Monolink, Monkey Safari and YokoO, remixed Ben Böhmer, and been remixed by Rodriguez Jr., Gabriel Ananda and Wankelmut. In 2024 he founded his own label, NASAJA.

        Away from the stage he is a radiation oncologist with a doctorate on glioblastoma brain tumours. He teaches medical students at the university clinic in Halle, still brings his violin to patients, and is founder and CCO of WeR1, a music platform built to pay artists more fairly.
